summary: You reached the optimal single-pass hash map solution and got full correctness (10/10 tests), including duplicates and index handling. The main gap was that you initially started with brute force and needed targeted hints to pivot to the complement-lookup pattern. Once on the right track, you implemented cleanly and stated correct complexity.

test_results.summary_note: All visible and hidden tests passed; no failures.

dimensions.name: Correctness & Completeness
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: Returned correct indices for all tests and avoided using the same element twice by checking the complement before inserting the current element. Correctly handles duplicate values (e.g., [3,3]) via storing prior index in the map.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Given the prompt guarantees exactly one answer, consider whether you want to return immediately (as you did) or raise/handle the no-solution case explicitly—be consistent with the expected contract instead of returning an empty list by default.

dimensions.name: Problem-Solving & Thinking
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You recognized the brute-force approach would be too slow under the constraints and successfully transitioned to a linear-time strategy once the key idea (complement lookup) clicked.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Practice articulating the invariant earlier: “when at index i, if I’ve stored all prior values, then any solution pair ending at i can be detected by checking target - nums[i] in O(1).” Getting to that framing faster reduces reliance on hints.

dimensions.name: Technical Communication
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You communicated uncertainty clearly and confirmed complexity accurately as O(n) time and O(n) space after implementing the hash map approach.
dimensions.what_to_improve: When stuck, narrate what information you need at each step (e.g., “I need to know if I’ve seen a number that pairs with the current one”)—this tends to lead you to the data structure choice without external prompting.

dimensions.name: Complexity & Optimization
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: Final approach matches the answer key optimal solution: single pass with hash map, O(n) time and O(n) space, which is appropriate for n up to 1e5.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Add a quick note about why average-case hash lookups are O(1) and acknowledge worst-case caveats briefly; interviewers like hearing the justification, not just the big-O.

dimensions.name: Code Quality
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: Code is concise, readable, and uses clear variable names (seen, complement). The check-before-insert ordering is correct and avoids self-pairing bugs.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Consider adding a short docstring or comment describing the invariant (“seen maps value -> index for prior elements”), and optionally return a tuple for indices if the platform expects immutability—small clarity/contract improvements.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: After receiving hints, you independently implemented the correct optimal algorithm and validated it with tests.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Work on generating the “complement in hash map” insight without prompting: when you see “two numbers sum to target,” default to asking yourself “can I rewrite it as x = target - y and track previous y’s?”

thinking_and_logic: You began with a straightforward nested-loop plan, then adjusted once performance concerns surfaced. With guidance, you adopted the key invariant: while scanning left-to-right, store previously seen values with their indices; for each current number n at index i, the only needed check is whether target - n already exists among prior values. This ensures you find the unique valid pair without reusing the same element, and it correctly handles duplicates due to storing indices.
code_assessment: Your final code implements the canonical optimal solution from the answer key: a one-pass hash map (value -> index) with complement check before insertion. This directly avoids common pitfalls listed in the key (same-element reuse and duplicate handling). Compared to the brute-force baseline, it improves time from O(n^2) to O(n) at the cost of O(n) extra space, which is the expected tradeoff for this problem class.

next_steps.action: Drill the “complement hash map” pattern across variants (Two Sum, Two Sum II/Sorted, 3Sum warmups).
next_steps.why: You got to the optimal approach, but only after hints; repetition builds the reflex to jump to the right invariant early.
next_steps.how: Do 5–10 problems where you transform a condition into “need to know if something previously seen exists” and solve with a map/set; write the invariant as the first comment before coding.

next_steps.action: Practice explaining invariants + complexity out loud in 30 seconds.
next_steps.why: Even with correct code, interview performance improves when you can justify correctness and big-O crisply.
next_steps.how: Use a template: (1) what’s stored, (2) what check is done each iteration, (3) why it guarantees a solution, (4) time/space with one sentence of justification.

next_steps.why: The answer key follow-up expects recognizing when you can do O(1) extra space with two pointers in a sorted array.
next_steps.how: Implement the two-pointer version returning indices (or 1-based if specified), and contrast it with the hash map approach in terms of space and constraints (sorted vs unsorted).

encouragement: You finished with the exact optimal solution and full test pass—focus now on building the reflex to reach that approach earlier and to explain the invariant confidently without needing hints.
